Nepal’s recent catastrophic floods, which have killed more than 1,340 people and left nearly 5,000 missing, according to the country’s disaster management agency, could change the way the world confronts the mounting climate-driven losses of developing nations.

Later this month, Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah will make his first foreign trip six months after taking office, traveling to New York to lead a small delegation to the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly. title: Hydropower Worker Survives 10 Days in Flooded Tunnel in Nepal - UA.NEWS
description: Hydropower Worker Survives 10 Days in Flooded Tunnel in Nepal  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
In Nepal, Sanjay Saha, a worker on a hydropower project, was rescued from a flooded tunnel after 10 days in darkness. He became trapped during the catastrophic flood on August 26, caused by the collapse of a glacial mountain on the border between China and Nepal.

As Channel NewsAsia reports, citing AFP, the 30-year-old Saha was pulled from the tunnel on September 4. After being rescued, he first asked rescuers how much time had passed. According to him, he believed he had been trapped for only several days.

Flooding at hydropower facilities

Saha was among hundreds of workers at several hydropower projects affected by the flood. He said that workers received a warning about the approaching water and tried to evacuate their colleagues, but there was not enough time. According to him, within minutes the tunnel was engulfed by raging water with waves several meters high.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

The Nepalese government linked the scale of the disaster to the consequences of rising global temperatures for the Himalayas. According to the data cited in the report, the disaster claimed at least 1,429 lives, while more than 5,640 people were considered missing; most of them were in Nepal.

Muddy water and contact with a colleague

Saha said he had no clean water and drank muddy water. In the darkness, he prayed and recited Hindu mantras, which, he said, helped him not lose hope. Nearby, 45-year-old worker Kabir Maharjan also survived. The men were separated but were able to speak to each other.

After several days in a Kathmandu hospital, Saha was returning to his home district of Saptari. He urged that search and rescue operations in the tunnels not be stopped. According to the outlet, rescuers saved another worker from China on September 5, but since then they have recorded no signs of life from other people.

title: Families await news of 55 Malaysians missing after Nepal floods - mediaselangor.com
description: Families await news of 55 Malaysians missing after Nepal floods  mediaselangor.com
publisher.title: mediaselangor.com
full_article:
SHAH ALAM, Sept 13 – The families and next-of-kin of 55 Malaysians who remain missing following the massive floods in Nepal continue to await the latest updates from the authorities, 19 days after the incident occurred.

The wife of Senior Fire Officer II Mohd Fakhrul Munir Mohd Isa, Hani Othman, said the families have yet to receive results regarding the DNA matching between relatives in Malaysia and the remains of victims in Nepal, *Berita Harian* reported.

However, Hani understood that the process is still ongoing.

"There are no updates yet on the DNA matching test. But I am told it is still in progress.

“I am still hoping for a miracle, yet I remain resigned to whatever outcome may come," she said when contacted.

On August 28, Hani reportedly flew to Kathmandu on her own to obtain direct updates on the search operations for her husband and other victims who remained out of contact.

She said she wanted to be closer to the search operations rather than simply waiting for updates from Malaysia.

When asked about the conclusion of the Special Malaysia Disaster Assistance and Rescue Team (SMART) MAS-01 mission in Nepal, Hani declined to comment further.

"I don't know how to comment. I have to be mindful of various parties; this issue is very sensitive," she said.

P. Sivan, 72, the father of Rajita Sivan said that DNA samples from the next-of-kin have already been collected, and the family is now awaiting further updates from Wisma Putra.

"The DNA has been collected. We are waiting for news from Wisma Putra. I hope (the victims) are found so that the DNA matching can be carried out.

"If they are found alive, it would be a miracle," he said.

A total of 55 Malaysians were reported to be out of contact following the disaster.



Another 77 Malaysians who were located safe in Tibet and Nepal, have been brought to Kathmandu to undergo processing before returning to Malaysia.

title: 'Nepal's mountains are not closed,' says new NTB board member Pemba Sherpa from Manaslu - The Tourism Times
description: 'Nepal's mountains are not closed,' says new NTB board member Pemba Sherpa from Manaslu  The Tourism Times
publisher.title: The Tourism Times
full_article:
KATHMANDU: Nepal’s mountains remain open to climbers and trekkers despite the recent devastation in Rasuwa and along the Bhotekoshi corridor, said newly appointed Nepal Tourism Board member Pemba Sherpa from Manaslu Base Camp.

Sherpa, who is in the base camp on behalf of the NTB to monitor mountaineering activity, said more than 400 climbers were currently there as the autumn climbing season got underway.

“Our mountains are not closed. We are open,” Sherpa said in a message from the base camp, urging international visitors not to stop travelling to Nepal following the recent floods.

According to the Department of Tourism, 451 climbers have received permits to climb Manaslu this autumn, making it by far the busiest mountain in Nepal’s current climbing season. Sherpa said the number of climbers and mountain guides involved in the season would exceed 1,000.

His remarks come weeks after devastating floods in Rasuwa and along the Bhotekoshi River disrupted communities and raised concerns about the impact on Nepal’s tourism industry.

“Please do visit our country, love our country, continue your climbing, continue your trekking, continue your journey,” Sherpa said. “We will support you.”

He said continued travel to Nepal would benefit the country while also supporting guides and other tourism workers whose livelihoods depend on trekking and mountaineering.

“This will be beneficial for the country, beneficial for the cause of flood relief and beneficial for our guides and their livelihood,” he said.

Sherpa is one of five private-sector members recently appointed to the NTB board. A director at 8K Expeditions, he has nearly 15 years of experience in Nepal’s tourism industry, including managing trekking and mountaineering expeditions and working as a general manager at a trekking agency.

Manaslu, the world’s eighth-highest mountain at 8,163 metres, has emerged as the main focus of Nepal’s autumn climbing season. The September 11 royalty report shows 451 climbers have been authorised to climb the mountain, generating $1.353 million in royalties.

title: Nepal Floods: 'Himalayas At Risk Of Cascading Disasters' - Rediff
description: Nepal Floods: 'Himalayas At Risk Of Cascading Disasters'  Rediff
publisher.title: Rediff
full_article:
Following Nepal's devastating floods, a senior Geological Survey of India official warns that the Himalayas are highly susceptible to cascading disasters, urging integrated scientific monitoring and preparedness to mitigate widespread destruction.

IMAGE: Members of the Nepal's Armed Police Force cross the Trishuli River via a temporary ropeway, in the aftermath of deadly flash floods and a mudslide, in Devighat, Bagmati Province, Nepal. Photograph: Anushree Fadnavis/Reuters

Key Points The Himalayas face a significant threat from cascading disasters, where a single high-altitude event can trigger a series of destructive phenomena like avalanches, river blockages, and flash floods, as seen in Nepal.

Assessing Himalayan hazards requires an integrated approach, combining satellite observations with on-ground field investigations and instrumentation to identify unstable mountain systems early.

Systematic scientific screening of high-risk areas, including deforming glaciers, unstable glacial lakes, and fractured rock slopes, is crucial for proactive disaster management.

The Indian Himalayas are particularly vulnerable due to their complex geology, rapidly flowing rivers, and concentrated settlements downstream, necessitating a shift to source-to-impact multi-hazard assessments.

Science-based preparedness, including sustained monitoring, data sharing, land-use planning, and community readiness, is essential to manage risks effectively rather than succumbing to alarm.

The Himalayas face the threat of a cascading disaster, where a single high-altitude calamity can trigger avalanches, block rivers and unleash flash floods, rapidly magnifying destruction downstream -- a danger laid bare by Nepal's recent catastrophe, said a senior Geological Survey of India official.

Therefore, Himalayan hazards cannot be assessed in isolation, he pointed out and stressed the need for combining satellite-based observations with field investigations and ground instrumentation.

A case in point is the Nepal disaster that appears to have involved cascading processes.

Satellite analysis identified an impoundment near the Langtang Lirung ice-rock avalanche site, with imagery of August 28 showing an approximately 11-hectare water impounded area. This provides evidence that the initial ice-rock failure was associated with temporary obstruction and water accumulation in the river system, said Pradeep Singh, the ADG of Policy Support System at the Geological Survey of India.

The flash floods near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26 devastated towns and villages in northern and central Nepal.

The Bhotekoshi river carried the floodwaters downstream, sweeping away homes, roads and bridges and killing more than 1,300 people.

Understanding Cascading Disasters in the Himalayas

Singh stressed the need to identify unstable mountain systems before they turn into catastrophic events.

"A single instability at high elevation can initiate a sequence involving an avalanche, landslide or glacier failure, river blockage, dam-break type release, debris flow and downstream flooding. Such processes can interact and amplify one another," he told PTI.

The geologist said the priority should be systematic scientific screening of potentially high-risk areas, particularly locations where a high-altitude failure could rapidly enter a river and affect populations and infrastructure downstream.

"The immediate priority should be a systematic, science-based screening of potentially high-risk source areas, rather than assuming that a similar catastrophic event will occur everywhere."

He pointed out that such screening should prioritise rapidly deforming glacier margins and glacier-rock systems, unstable and moraine-dammed glacial lakes, steep and fractured rock slopes, locations showing persistent or accelerating deformation in satellite observations, and valleys where a high-altitude failure could rapidly propagate downstream.

Glacial lakes are formed by melting glaciers accumulating in depressions on or near the glacier's surface. Glacial Lake Outburst Floods occur when these lakes suddenly burst open due to factors such as excessive water accumulation or earthquakes.

One such outburst in Sikkim in October 2023 resulted in at least 60 fatalities and extensive damage in four districts.

Integrating Satellite Data and Ground Investigations

Singh said, "Satellite observations can potentially provide valuable precursor information, particularly where progressive deformation or acceleration occurs before failure. However, a detected increase in movement indicates that the particular slope is in distress; however, the failure will occur on reaching the limit equilibrium condition, which may be difficult to predict."

The answer lies in combining satellite-based observations with field investigations and ground instrumentation.

Singh asserted that the most effective approach was not to rely on a single satellite indicator, but to integrate multi-temporal InSAR, optical feature tracking, DEM differencing, field instrumentation and ground observations.

This would allow authorities to build a regional inventory of anomalous or rapidly deforming glacier-rock, moraine and slope systems and focus detailed investigations and monitoring on locations with potentially serious downstream consequences.

"The objective should be to identify potentially unstable systems early, understand how they may fail, estimate their possible downstream effects and establish an appropriate level of monitoring and preparedness."

Himalayan Vulnerabilities and Preparedness in India

Singh said the concern was particularly relevant for the Indian segment of the Himalayas because the region combines glaciers, steep and fractured rock slopes, permafrost-affected terrain, glacial lakes, unstable moraines and rapidly flowing rivers, while settlements and critical infrastructure are often concentrated downstream.

"The key shift required is from hazard-by-hazard assessment to source-to-impact multi-hazard assessment. It allows authorities to understand not only where instability may occur, but also what could happen next and who or what may be exposed downstream," he said.

He, however, cautioned against interpreting the Nepal disaster as proof that every Himalayan town in India faces an imminent glacier-related catastrophe.

"Risk in India is highly site-specific and depends on local geology, slope stability, glacier and glacial-lake conditions, hydrology, climate, terrain and patterns of human development."

He said there were nevertheless reasons for vigilance on changing glacier conditions, expanding or unstable glacial lakes and moraines, possible permafrost degradation at high elevations, steep and fractured slopes, intense rainfall, landslides and debris flows, as well as increasing infrastructure, settlement and tourism in valleys.

GSI is undertaking landslide susceptibility assessments and glaciological studies in the Himalayas, Singh said, adding that these data should be integrated with satellite deformation monitoring, glacial-lake inventories, geophysical studies and flood and debris-flow modelling. GSI studies of nine Himalayan glaciers have recorded overall negative average annual specific mass balance, indicative of substantial glacier mass wastage under changing climatic conditions.

"For India, the appropriate response is not alarm, but science-based preparedness. The objective is not to eliminate the mountains' natural processes, but to understand them better, identify highly vulnerable areas, reduce exposure and improve available response time.

"With sustained scientific monitoring, improved data sharing, appropriate land-use planning, robust infrastructure and community preparedness, risks can be better managed," Singh added.

title: Yatri Motorcycles launches P2 electric motor scooter in Nepal - THE PACK – Electric motorcycle news
description: Yatri Motorcycles launches P2 electric motor scooter in Nepal  THE PACK – Electric motorcycle news
publisher.title: THE PACK – Electric motorcycle news
full_article:
Nepali manufacturer Yatri Motorcycles has introduced the P2, a new electric scooter designed and built domestically for the country’s roads and climbing conditions.

Powertrain and range

The P2 uses a high-power mid-drive PMSM motor rated at 10 kW peak, producing 315 Nm of torque at the wheel. Top speed is listed at 90 km/h. Power runs through a 7.12 final drive ratio via a high-efficiency chain, controlled by a power-dense 680A three-phase AC controller with active cooling intended to sustain continuous hill climbing.

Range is rated at up to 207 km with a range extender fitted. Yatri quotes DC fast charging to 80 percent in 41 minutes, and backs the battery with an 8-year or 80,000 km warranty.

Charging infrastructure

Yatri is pairing the P2 with its own DC charging network, using what it calls a Plug-and-Charge protocol: the charger’s CMS and the scooter’s VCU handle authentication and session management automatically. The companion app shows real-time charger data, including live availability, distance, and estimated travel time to nearby stations.

Connectivity and instrumentation

The P2 is fitted with a 7-inch programmable LED TFT instrument cluster. Listed connected features include wireless CarPlay, connected media, ride intelligence, tyre pressure monitoring, and a smart charger finder. A companion app tracks live vehicle data, battery status, and range remotely.

Safety systems

Yatri lists several electronic safety features on the P2: fall detection that cuts power to the drivetrain in the event of a crash, an emergency response function that shares the rider’s location with emergency contacts, remote immobilization, and movement tracking to flag unexpected relocation of the vehicle. Lighting includes Class-D headlamps and a smart tail light.

Availability

The P2 is available to book now in Nepal, with test rides offered through Yatri’s dealer network. Yatri Motorcycles is based in Budhanilkantha, Kathmandu.

Work to rebuild trade routes destroyed by catastrophic flooding in Nepal has begun, with a new bridge across the Tadi River that the Nepali Army is calling the "bridge of hope." The structural installation reconnects essential supply lines following widespread destruction across the mountain nation.

Nepal will need significant resources as the country starts digging itself out of a disaster-related economic crisis. Government officials estimate the recovery process will cost at least $5 billion in reconstruction receipts alone.

What the headline number does not account for, industry experts said, is the knock-on impacts from losing critical infrastructure the country depends on for travel and transporting goods.

The physical damage to transportation corridors, energy networks, and civil structures presents a complex engineering challenge for local authorities. Rebuilding damaged mountain roads requires specialized equipment, reinforced retaining walls, and resilient structural designs capable of withstanding future severe environmental events.

Developing durable crossings remains a central technical priority for engineering crews working in high-risk topography across the region. Military personnel and civilian contractors are coordinating efforts to restore primary transit arteries, clear earth slide debris, and stabilize weakened slopes adjacent to major highways.

Emergency infrastructure projects, such as modular steel truss installations and temporary earthworks, are being deployed to re-establish access for remote communities. Local authorities are prioritizing the restoration of freight access along primary arterial paths to ensure food, medical provisions, and raw construction materials reach inland distribution hubs.

Foreign assistance and climate finance mechanisms are expected to play a role in funding heavy civil engineering works and regional grid repairs across impacted river basins.

Planning agencies face steep financial hurdles as they map out multi-year infrastructure rehabilitation programs across the affected provinces. Rebuilding primary logistical networks remains essential to restoring internal commerce and supporting regional trade flows.

Engineers and planners continue evaluating damage across regional road networks, bridge abutments, and hydroelectric infrastructure damaged during the recent surge of high-volume runoff.

Restoring stable connectivity across vulnerable river crossings like the Tadi River remains vital for long-term economic stability and basic transit operations across Nepal.

description: Nepal Tunnel Survivor Finds Solace in Village Homecoming  usnews.com
publisher.title: usnews.com
full_article:
By Sahana Bajracharya

TILATHI KOILADI, Nepal, Sept 13 (Reuters) - After nine days ⁠trapped ⁠in a hydropower tunnel and a ⁠week of hospital care following his dramatic rescue, Sanjay Sah, a rare survivor ​of last month's devastating glacier collapse in Nepal, finally returned to his village and family on Sunday.

It was a homecoming ‌marked by relief and joy but also ‌grief.

"I was trapped in the tunnel ... I felt trapped in the hospital room too. I finally feel free ⁠here in ⁠my village," Sah, 30, said after arriving in Tilathi Koiladi, near the border ​with India.

At least 1,386 people have died and 5,130 are still missing across Nepal weeks after a Himalayan glacier collapsed near the Chinese border, unleashing a wall of mud and water that crashed through mountain valleys destroying everything in its path.

Around 900 ​power station workers remain missing. Sah, a mechanical foreman at the Upper Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station, was ⁠one ⁠of just three pulled from ⁠debris-buried tunnels extending ​deep under the mountains.

He survived in the darkness, drinking flood water and seepage from the mountain rock until ​rescue workers finally reached him.

Sah ⁠left the hospital in the capital Kathmandu on Friday and the next day boarded a bus for an overnight journey home.

A TEARFUL HOMECOMING TO A VILLAGE STILL IN MOURNING

Around 60 people, mostly women, awaited his arrival in Tilathi Koiladi on Sunday.

Family members, including his parents, uncle, wife and daughter, performed a traditional welcome ceremony, washing his feet as ⁠part of a cleansing ritual.

After his mother dabbed a pink vermilion tika on his forehead, Sah ⁠bowed. They embraced and then broke down in tears.

"My son!" his mother cried, holding him tightly and kissing him on the cheek.

Women who had gathered to witness the reunion used their colourful saris to wipe the tears from their eyes.

Many in Tilathi Koiladi are still awaiting word of the fate of family members who had been working at hydropower stations hit by the flooding.

"There are more people from my village still missing after the flood," Sah told Reuters.

One family, he said, phoned him while he was still in the hospital to ask if he had seen or heard from ⁠a missing relative who had been working at a different power station. He had to tell them he had not.

At home among family, Sah said he is ready to put his ordeal behind him.

"I will stay in my village for some time now. I want to meet all my people," ​he said. "But if I am called back to duty, I will go."

(Reporting by Sahan ​Bajracharya in eastern Nepal; Writing by Krishna N. Das;)

After flash floods isolated parts of Nepal's mountain border region, cargo drones have taken on jobs that are too risky or difficult to handle on foot, including flying food to stranded survivors and recovering bodies from places that are hard to access.

Here's what to know

After flooding hit the Nepal-Tibet border zone, Nepal's army began using four DJI FlyCart 100 drones donated by China, Reuters reported.

On August 26, part of a Himalayan glacier gave way, triggering a rush of water, mud, and debris. The surge tore through border crossings, valley communities, and hydropower sites, leaving many areas difficult to reach by land.

As rescue teams continue searching remote areas for survivors, the International Organization for Migration is seeking $20.5 million in aid for 43,000 people affected by the flooding in Nepal.

Drones are already a key part of the response in delivering supplies, but their use is increasing for other tasks. Reuters noted they can also be used for reconnaissance, and for transporting the bodies of flood victims.

On August 26, 2026, a series of avalanches, flash floods, and debris flows in Nepal and Tibet left an estimated 1,400 people dead, with another 5,850 still missing. Dubbed the 2026 Nepal-China floods, the disaster destroyed the China-Nepal Gyirong checkpoint and devastated dozens of settlements along a 45-mile (72 km) stretch of the Trishuli River.

The event also severely damaged around a dozen hydropower plants, constituting around 10% of Nepal’s total power production. According to reports, it is not yet clear if the damage can be repaired.
